Write $B=T^3$, and let $B^j$ be its j-fold iterate. A start $n$ has $m$ good blocks if $B^j(n)\equiv11\pmod{16}$ for every $j<m$.

For every natural $m>0$,

$$
\exists n\in\mathbb N,\quad (\forall j<m,\ B^j(n)\equiv11\pmod{16})\ \land\ n<B^m(n).
$$

Choose $n=16\cdot8^m-5$. The seed recurrence verifies all m good blocks and gives the final value $16\cdot9^m-5$. The strict comparison follows from $9^m>8^m$ for positive m.

$$
b^k\le d x_0+c.
$$

Set $y_i=d x_i+c$. Multiplying the affine equation by $d$ and adding $bc$ gives $b y_{i+1}=(b+d)y_i$. Apply the finite coprime-multiplier bound to this shifted sequence.

Let $C:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ be the ordinary Collatz map: $C(n)=n/2$ for even $n$ and $C(n)=3n+1$ for odd $n$. Write $C^k$ for its $k$-fold iterate.

Universal descent means that each $n>1$ has a positive time $k$ with $C^k(n)<n$. Then

$$
\bigl(\forall n>1,\ \exists k>0,\ C^k(n)<n\bigr)\iff\bigl(\forall n>0,\ \exists j\in\mathbb N,\ C^j(n)=1\bigr).
$$

Convergence implies descent by using the iterate reaching 1. Conversely, strong induction sends each start above 1 to a strictly smaller positive iterate, applies convergence there, and concatenates the two finite trajectories.

Let $a,b,c$ be positive natural numbers satisfying

$$2^{b+c}+3\,2^b=2^{a+b}+3\,2^a.$$

Then

$$a=b\quad\text{and}\quad b=c.$$

This is the arithmetic obstruction for the particular two-center, three-edge ansatz described in the source: its displayed consistency equation allows no distinct positive labels. The theorem does not assert existence of a Collatz trajectory or settle termination.

Proof. Factor the equation as 2^b(2^c+3)=2^a(2^b+3). Positivity of b and c makes the parenthesized factors odd. Odd-part uniqueness gives b=a and equality of those factors. Removing the common three gives 2^c=2^b, and odd-part uniqueness with odd factor one gives c=b. $$2^R A=2^S B\quad\Longrightarrow\quad R=S\ \text{and}\ A=B.$$

Oddness makes both factors positive, so no separate nonzero assumption is needed. This is uniqueness of the power-of-two times odd-part representation; it is a reusable arithmetic lemma.

$$\forall x,y\in X,\qquad I(x)=I(y).$$
